1: Determination of the Maximum Specific Uptake Capacities for Glucose and Oxygen in Glucose-Limited Fed-Batch Cultivations of Escherichia coli H. Y. Lin1 B. Mathiszik1 B. Xu2* S.-O. Enfors3 P. Neubauer1† 1Martin-Luther-Universita ̈ t Halle-Wittenberg Fachbereich Biochemie/ Biotechnologie Institut fu ̈ r Biotechnologie D-06099 Halle Germany 2Royal Institute of Technology Dept. of Biotechnology S-10044 Stockholm Sweden Received 20 January 2000; accepted 31 October 2000 Abstract: A simple pulse-based method for the determi- nation of the maximum uptake capacities for glucose and oxygen in glucose limited cultivations of E. coli is pre- sented. The method does not depend on the time- consuming analysis of glucose or acetate and therefore can be used to control the feed rate in glucose limited cultivations such as fed-batch processes. The applica- tion of this method in fed-batch processes of E. coli showed that the uptake capacity for neither glucose nor oxygen is a constant parameter as often is assumed in fed-batch models. The glucose uptake capacity de- creased significantly when the specific growth rate de- creased below 0.15 h-1 and fell to about 0.6 mmol g-1 h-1 (mmol per g cell dry weight and hour) at the end of fed- batch fermentations where μ was approximately 0.02 h-1. The oxygen uptake capacity started to decrease somewhat earlier when μ declined below 0.25 h -1 and was 5 mmol g-1 h-1 at the end of the fermentations. The behavior of both uptake systems is integrated in a dynamic model which allows a better fitting of ex- perimental values for glucose in fed-batch processes in comparison to generally used unstructured kinetic models. © 2001 John Wiley & Sons Inc. Keywords: fed-batch-fermentation; kinetic model; ac- etate; oxygen uptake; dissolved oxygen tension INTRODUCTION Overflow of acetate in aerobic glucose-based cultures of E. coli occurs when the specific glucose uptake is greater than the conversion of glucose to biomass and carbon dioxide. The rate-limiting steps contributing to acetate production have been attributed to either the electron transport system (El-Mansi and Holms 1989) or to the TCA cycle (Holms 1986; Majewski and Domach 1990a). Acetate production is often considered to be a problem in E. coli processes as it has been reported to inhibit growth (Luli and Strohl 1990; Shimizu et al. 1988) or to reduce recombinant protein pro- duction (Jensen and Carlsen 1990; MaDonald and Neway 1990). Therefore specific fermentation strategies as well as metabolic approaches have been used to decrease the pro- duction of acetate (Bauer et al. 1990; Chou et al. 1994ab; Jung et al. 1988; Konstantinov et al. 1990; San et al. 1994; Shimizu et al. 1988). Kinetic models of microbial processes mostly consider qOmax and q Smax as constant parameters. Thereby the dif- ference between simulation curves and experimental results is neglected as presented and discussed by Xu et al. (1999). By using such unstructured models it is ignored that meta- bolic studies of E. coli data are known which clearly show that both parameters dynamically change with the specific growth rate (Hunter and Kornberg 1979; Neijssel et al. 1977 1980). From these studies it is known that the cellular content of the glucose:phosphoenolpyruvate phosphotrans- ferase system (glucose-PTS) in E. coli varies proportionally with the specific growth rate (Neijssel et al. 1980) which is different from Klebsiella aerogenes. The total glucose up- take capacity measured by addition of an unsaturating glu- cose pulse to a glucose-limited chemostat culture was only about 60% of the maximum rate but increased progres- sively as the dilution rate in the chemostat was increased. Hunter and Kornberg (1979) showed that the total PTS ac- tivity in vitro increased up to a growth rate of 0.3 h -1 but is not further increased at higher growth rates which the authors explain as a result of the added activities of the high-affinity glucose-PTS and the low-affinity mannose- PTS. Consistent in these studies is that a glucose pulse also stimulated the respiratory activity (Hunter and Kornberg 1979; Neijssel et al. 1977). The problem of applying the published data which origi- nate from chemostat experiments to models which can be used in the process development or directly in industrial processes is that these parameters depend on the specific strains and the cultivation conditions. Whereas a number of transient models for Saccharomyces cerevisiae have been published (e.g. Duboc et al. 1998) corresponding models of E. coli are limited. Therefore it was the aim of this study to develop a method which can be easily applied to determine the capac- ity for the glucose uptake and oxygen consumption in the dynamic environment of glucose-limited fed-batch pro- cesses. Åkesson et al. (1999ab) applied feeding strategies which implied pulses of the feeding solution to get information for the optimum feed rate and detect the feed range where no acetate is produced (see also Åkesson 1999). Also Kon- stantinov et al. (1990) adjusted the feed according to the critical specific glucose uptake rate by a closed-loop control algorithm to take the decreasing respiratory capacity into account. In contrast to these studies which aimed at an optimum feed rate to avoid acetate formation the objective of this study was the determination of the actual uptake capacities for oxygen and glucose in fed-batch processes. The calcu- lation of these parameters is of special interest for the char- acterization and optimization of fed-batch processes by ki- netic models. Therefore we propose a model which con- siders the changing capacities for glucose and oxygen uptake and thus enables a better fit of experimental glucose data. A cultivation in 10 mL of nutrient broth (NBII: 1% tryptone 0.6% yeast extract) was followed by culture in a shake flask containing the fermentation medium (200 mL medium i n 1 L Erlenmeyer flasks with baffles at 37°C at 165 rpm in a rotary shaker). Each preculture was used at the exponential growth phase as inoculum for the next cultiva- tion. All fermentations were performed in either a 15 L or a 6 L Biostat ED fermenter (B. Braun Biotech International Germany) with a starting volume of 7 L or 4 L respectively (temperature 35°C pH 7.0). The pH was controlled to drop not below 7.0 by addition of 25% ammonia. Air flow (0.002 to 2 vvm) and stirrer speed (200 to 800 rpm) were controlled in a cascade mode during the batch phase to keep the dis- solved oxygen tension (DOT) above 20%. The MFCS-Win supervisory system (v. 1.1 B. Braun Biotech Int. Germany) was used for data collection. Two different fermentation protocols were used. The first protocol was applied according to Xu et al. (1999). This fermentation was started with a working volume of 7 L. The cultivation was initially running as a batch for 0.92 h. Than an exponential glucose feed was started (initial feed rate 5.7 mL h-1 exponential rate constant 0.27 h -1) which was ap- plied for 9.1 h. When the feed rate reached a rate of 64 mL h-1 it was kept constant for 2.5 h. Afterwards a lower constant feed rate of 57 mL h -1 was applied up to the end of the cultivation. The second protocol was applied according to Teich et al. (1998). In this case after an initial batch phase to an optical cell density (OD500) of 8 the feeding pump was started at a constant rate of 53.2 mL h -1 which was maintained to the end of the cultivation. Analytical Methods Cellular Growth Growth of the cultures was followed by measuring the op- tical density at 500 nm (OD 500). One unit of OD 500 corre- sponds to a cell dry weight of 0.24 g L -1. DOT The dissolved oxygen tension was measured by a polaro- graphic DOT electrode (Mettler-Toledo no. 322336110) with a response time of 45-60 sec (98% manufacturer in- structions). Glucose Uptake Capacity During the batch phase the glucose uptake capacity (q Scap) was calculated from the uptake kinetiks of glucose. In fed- batch conditions where glucose was limiting the growth pulses of glucose (0.5-1 g L -1 final concentration) were added to the cultivations. q Scap was then calculated from analyzed samples which were frequently collected after the pulse as well as from the DOT curve after the pulse if the respiration was not limiting as described in Results. The medium samples were directly sucked from the reactor through a 0.2 mm disc filter into a syringe (Monovette Sarstedt). Glucose and Acetate The analysis of glucose was performed with the hexokinase/ glucose-6-phosphate-dehydrogenase method (Kit No. 139106 Boehringer Mannheim GmbH Germany) scaled down to microtiter plates with four parallels for each sample as described by Larsson and To ̈rnkvist (1996). Acetate was analyzed with Kit no. 148261 (Boehringer Mannheim GmbH Germany). Outgas Analysis The outgas oxygen and carbon dioxide concentrations were measured with an URAS10E (Hartmann & Braun GmbH Frankfurt Germany) which was placed close to the fer- menter. The specific rates (q Oq CO2) were calculated con- tinuously over the fermentation by including the fitted bio- mass values and the actual reactor volume which was cal- culated from the total reactor weight corrected for the broth density. Modeling and Computer Simulation For simulation of the fermentations the SCILAB program (INRIA www.inria.fr) was used. The model applied is de- scribed in Results. RESULTS The Model Fed-Batch Process Typical glucose-limited fed-batch cultivations of E. coli with different feeding strategies are shown in Figures 1 and 2. Figure 1 shows a fed-batch with an initial exponential feed phase which after 10 h was changed to a constant feed. Whereas in this case glucose limits the growth during the whole process with exception of the initial 4 h the culti- vation in Figure 2 starts with a batch phase on an initial glucose concentration of5gL -1. In this cultivation the cells grow at the maximum specific growth rate for a longer period. The batch phase was then directly followed by a glucose-limited fed-batch phase with a constant feed rate of the glucose solution. After feed start the specific growth rate declined gradually. 4: model published by Xu et al. (1999). The parameters used in the simulations are shown in Table I and the resulting simulation plots are shown in Figures 1 and 2. By compari- son of the simulation plots with the experimental data it is remarkable that all experimental data are nicely fitted by the model during the batch phase but significant deviations occur in the fed-batch part. Major deviations of the model from the analyses are observed for glucose and acetate. Although the glucose concentration in the medium is con- stant with a slight tendency to increase all kinetic models used so far show a continuous decrease of the glucose con- centration as they are based on the MONOD equation. Simi- larly the acetate values are very low up to the end of the fermentation but sometimes increase in the final phase of a fed-batch and this is also not reflected in the models. In the fermentation of Figure 2 we added a number of glucose pulses to the cultivation. The corresponding re- sponse to the calculated q O data does not agree with the simulation (see Fig. 2E). According to the model q O should increase to q Omax after each pulse independent of the time of its addition. However as the response of q O becomes lower the later in the process the pulse is added one could assume that qOmax or according to our nomenclature qOcap is not constant. Although it can be found in the literature that neither qSmax nor qOcap are constants (Hunter and Korn- berg 1979; Neijssel et al. 1977 1980) this has never been confirmed in kinetic models to our knowledge. One limita- tion for the application of the growth rate-dependent data for qScap and qOcap from the literature is that they cannot be easily used in a dynamic model because they originate from chemostat experiments. In contrast to the steady-state con- ditions in a chemostat in fed-batch fermentations the popu- lation of cells is characterized by its history which is char- acterized by the specific feeding profile. Therefore we con- sidered a method to measure qScap and qOcap in a simple way under process conditions. Interestingly this easy method was not applied to glucose-limited fed-batch fermentations to our knowl- edge. However Åkesson et al. (1999ab) performed re- peated shifts in the feed rate to estimate the optimum feed rate from the reaction of the DOT but they did not saturate the glucose uptake system which is a requirement for the calculation of uptake capacity. In order to estimate the maximum rate of glucose uptake we performed glucose pulses which oversaturate the glu- cose uptake system. After the addition of a pulse of 0.5 to 2 gL -1 of glucose fast medium samples were taken in the minutes time range from the reactor to estimate the glucose consumption rate. However this method is inaccurate time- consuming and difficult to automate. Therefore we looked for simple on-line signals which could be used for the es- timation of q Scap. One of the fast-responding signals is the DOT. In our bioreactor we use the MFCS Win supervisory system (B. Braun Melsungen Germany) with an event- based data-storing strategy. The data storage interval is de- pendent on the minimum time interval for data collection and the selected minimum deviation of the specific param- eter which is the signal for faster data storage and can be separately selected for each single parameter. In our system the minimum data-storing interval was set to 5 sec and the sensitivity for the DOT to 0.1% change which allows a fast data collection when the DOT electrode is responding to a nutrient shift. As shown in Figure 3A the DOT decreases very fast to a lower level after a glucose pulse at t p with a reaction time of the electrode of less than 2 sec. The de- crease of the DOT is followed by a second phase during which the DOT level is approximately constant as long as the glucose uptake is at the maximum rate. Later if the glucose approaches a level which is not saturating the up- take system (t R) the DOT begins to rise. For E. coli this DOT rise is very rapid at cell concentrations in the g cell dry weight per L range because of the very low K S value for glucose which is on the order of magnitude of a few mg L-1 (Neubauer et al. 1995). We found that it is possible to determine q Scap not only by the analysis of the medium glucose concentration but by the time interval between the response of the DOT signal after the glucose pulse (t P) and tR. The calculation of the glucose uptake capacity only by the DOT signal can be applied if the following restrictions are considered: 1) the method can be only applied if the growth is limited by glucose; 2) the actual respiration rate must be lower than the respiratory capacity so that a DOT decrease appears after glucose addition; and 3) the oxygen transfer capacity of the reactor has to be considered to avoid anaerobic conditions during the time of the pulse. The amount of glucose added to the reactor should be used within a few minutes to only marginally disturb the fed-batch process and to not have a major influence on cellular growth. Effect of Acetate In E. coli high uptake rates of glucose are normally con- nected to the formation of acetate as an overflow metabolite. The reason seems to be either a limited capacity of the respiratory system (Anderson and von Meyenburg 1980) or a limited capacity of the tricarbonic acid cycle (Majewski and Domach 1990b). Independent of the real point of limi- tation for growth models acetate formation has been con- nected to the relation between q Smax and qOcap (Hunter and Kornberg 1979). On the other side the consumption of acetate as a carbon source is also connected to respiration and therefore effects the DOT signal. Therefore a pulse of acetate to a glucose-limited fed-batch cultivation also gives a typical signal which however is very different from the signal of glucose (Fig. 5). This is because the rate of acetate uptake is generally low (about 0.15 g g -1 h-1) and also due to the formation of NADH 2 from acetate. Therefore the effect of acetate on the DOT is much lower than the effect of glucose. The DOT is decreasing by a lower rate after the acetate pulse. We did not see a constant low level of the DOT according to the phase 2 of a glucose pulse but the DOT increased directly after the curve showed a minimum. This is possibly connected to the different uptake kinetics of acetate from glucose which is characterized by facilitated diffusion and about a tenfold higher K S value. Acetate is also formed after a glucose pulse. However as the response is slow and the redirection of the acetate flow from production to consumption takes some time it does not disturb the DOT signal which is used for q Smax calcu- lation. However phase 3 of the DOT signal is dependent on the amount of acetate which appears as a shoulder and delays the return of the DOT to the prepulse value (see Figs. 3A 5B). Although we did not evaluate this the appropriate signal could surely be used for the calculation of the rates for acetate production and uptake. Interestingly external acetate addition directly after a glucose pulse as shown in Figure 5B causes a further in- crease of the q O value which further proves that q Ocap is a kinetic model constant which is determined by limitations in the tricarboxic acid cycle and not by limitations in the re- spiratory chain as extensively discussed e.g. by Majewski and Domach (1990a). This increase of the q O is only sig- nificant by externally added acetate but there is only a slight increase of qO if more acetate is accumulated in response to a larger glucose pulse (data not shown). We therefore as- sume that this qO increase is due to the uncoupling effect of acetate although the added acetate concentration was low in all cases (only 1.7 mM). Accordingly q Ocap can be detected by using the outgas oxygen signal. The q O calcu- lated from this signal follows the DOT curve and the maxi- mum corresponds to the maximum oxygen uptake rate. In dependence on whether the respiratory limi- tation is caused by a limited activity of the respiratory sys- tem or by a limited TCA cycle activity acetate formation or alternatively acetate addition may differently influence the qOcap value. This in our case is not visible in the q O curve; in contrast to Åkesson et al. (1998) the glucose pulses we use are relatively small and the outgas analysis is slightly slower than the DOT response. However q Ocap increases over the maximum value which is caused by the glucose pulse when acetate is added within the glucose pulse (see Fig. 5B). As we saw this behavior in early phases of the fed-batch fermentation as well as in the final phase of our fed-batch cultivations we conclude that TCA cycle limita- tion is responsible for the production of acetate and not a limitation in the respiratory system. However the actual investigations with the apparent q Ocap show that activity of the limiting reaction in the TCA must further decrease dur- ing the fed-batch fermentation. For the set-up of our fer- mentations similar to q Scapq Ocap was approximately con- stant between mmax and a m of 0.25 h -1. However when cells are grown at lower growth rates q Ocap decreases sig- nificantly (Fig. 6). To the end of the cultivation the process is controlled by the low rates of q Scap and qOcap. A glucose pulse at very low growth rates did not influence the DOT signal further although the analysis of the glucose concen- tration proves that the substrate is consumed (Fig. 7). How- ever we also did not find an elevated production of acetate which might indicate that the capacities of both systems are tuned to each other. However we also cannot exclude from our data production of other side metabolites such as lac- tate although in this case one should assume an increased addition of ammonia to keep the pH constant which was not the case in our studies (Fig. 7B). Structured Model for Growth-Related Adaptation of qScap and qOcap The foregoing experiments indicate that neither capacities for the specific glucose uptake nor for the specific oxygen uptake are constants in a process with a changing growth situation. Although we did not evaluate the limiting bio- chemical reactions for incorporation of this new data in a kinetic model it can be assumed that the amount of enzyme per cell is changing which is catalyzing the reactions for consumption of substrate (glucose) and oxygen (qO and qS) thereby ignoring the multistep reactions in the glucose PTS uptake system and in the respiratory chain. For simulations we used the model of Xu et al. (1999). This model allows a fairly good description of the glucose overflow metabolism in E. coli in dependence on the respi- ratory capacity (q Ocap). The glucose flux is directed to the oxidative metabolism and further divided into glucose for anabolic reactions (a) which finally accumulates as X q m (b) and energy formation q Soxen (c). Neither q m and qSoxen contribute to biomass carbon. The formation of acetate is controlled by the relation between the specific oxygen up- take rate (qO) and the cellular capacity for the specific oxy- gen uptake (qOcap) (see Appendix). It should be remarked that for a better description of the measured ac- etate concentrations the corresponding enzymatic kinetics could be incorporated similar to the enzyme kinetics for glucose and oxygen consumption. However such a model should include the regulations in the tricarbonic acid cycle by glucose and acetate which we will consider in the future but which is actually limited by the molecular physiological data available. Furthermore including a realistic response to acetate is much more complex because of the different ef- fects of high and low concentrations of acetate on the meta- bolic flows but also on the deregulation of the proton motive force. CONCLUSIONS The aim of this study was to address the question of varia- tion of the capacities for glucose and oxygen consumption in fed-batch cultivations for use in modeling. Therefore we developed an easy method which allows the fast determi- nation of the actual capacities for glucose uptake and oxy- gen consumption. Although we analyzed these values off- line after the fermentations the method in principle can be automated and could be used for on-line process control as the measured parameters are on-line values provided that an on-line biomass sensor is used. A similar pulse-based method was developed by Åkesson (1999; see also Åkesson et al. 1999b) who used changes of the glucose feed flow rate but different from our method they did not saturate the cellular glucose uptake system and therefore do not obtain the qScap and qOcap values. The results obtained with the glucose pulse method re- vealed that the maximum uptake rates for glucose and for oxygen are changing in a fed-batch process to lower values. As the change of these parameters can result in overfeeding and by this in the increase of glucose and acetate in the cultivation medium they are very important for the design of a feed strategy for a fed-batch fermentation. The change of these parameters to our knowledge has never been considered in kinetic models. We tried to simu- late the variation of the uptake behavior by assuming that the uptake capacities are controlled by the amount of en- zyme. This seems also to have physiological relevance as recently published by Plumbridge (1998) that the expres- sion of the ptsG gene coding for the glucose transporter of the glucose-PTS is positively regulated by glucose. In prin- cipal one alternatively could also assume a change of the KS value; however in our understanding the K S value is connected to the kinetics of the enzymatic reaction which is neglected to change in our model. Furthermore we do not consider that different glucose uptake systems exist in E. coli which are known to change in their concentration in dependence on the growth rate and which also have differ- ent affinities for glucose. In connection with respiration the efficiency of ATP generation from NADH2 can also change. However the limited knowledge about all the correspond- ing regulations in the frame of glucose uptake and respira- tion does not allow us at the moment to build a physiologi- cally based model which can easily be applied in process technology. Whereas the model improves the description of the be- havior of glucose in the fed-batch fermentations it does not satisfactorily describe the response of acetate. This could be due to the fact that the acetate uptake might be induced only if the acetate concentration is high enough as reported in Kleman and Strohl (1994).
